terms.gloss: take the place of, take over from, succeed
terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive; with the dative, or in locum and the genitive
evidence: Quint. 2.2.5: succēdere sē in eōrum locum … exīstimet
Caes. BG 5.16 (Lewis & Short): ut integrī et recentēs dēfatīgātīs succēderent
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to follow, follow after, take the place of, relieve”. A successor is successor (Ov. Met. 3.589).

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation (-iō); with in locum and the genitive
evidence: M-O s.v. replace (someone): in alicujus locum sufficī
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to choose or elect in the place of any one (class.; esp. freq. of magistrates)”: a consul elected in place of one who has died is cōnsul suffectus.

terms.gloss: act in place of, stand in for
evidence: Hor. Ars 304: ergō fungar vice cōtis
Traupman 22: locum mātris meae numquam ūsurpāre potest
terms.comment: Lewis & Short give ūsurpāre as “to make use of, to take possession of”, but not with locum in this sense; say in locum alicujus succēdere.

phrases.latin: sūmat igitur ante omnia parentis ergā discipulōs suōs animum, ac succēdere sē in eōrum locum, ā quibus sibi līberī trādantur, exīstimet
phrases.english: Let him first of all take on a parent’s feelings towards his pupils, and think of himself as taking the place of those who hand their children over to him.

phrases.latin: quippe et Rhō litterae, quā Dēmosthenēs quoque labōrāvit, Labda succēdit
phrases.english: for Lambda takes the place of the letter Rho, which even Demosthenes had trouble with

phrases.latin: interdum fessae succēdit laeva sorōrī alternatque vicēs
phrases.english: Now and then the left hand takes over from her tired sister, and they take turns.

sources: Lewis & Short: succedo · Lewis & Short: sufficio · Lewis & Short: vicis · Lewis & Short: fungor
